raw_case_text:
The patient's mother, a resident of Bouake, was 30 years old, with gravidity 4 and parity 2 (including a spontaneous abortion at 17 weeks). During the pregnancy, routine serological testing determined that she had sickle cell disease (type AS, S=79%), a rubella titer of 13 IU/mL, a toxoplasmosis IgG titer of 14 IU/mL, and that she was syphilis (Treponema pallidum haemagglutination [TPHA], venereal disease research laboratory [VDRL])-negative, hepatitis B- and C-negative, and HIV-negative. The mother had health insurance that allowed for nine prenatal consultations with accompanying obstetric ultrasounds. The radiologist reported no abnormalities during this time. The mother did not take any medication or drugs, and was not exposed to teratogens, toxins, or abnormal levels of radiation during the pregnancy. Moreover, no congenital abnormalities were noted.
After a gestational period of 39 weeks, the patient was delivered via cesarean section. The birth weight was recorded as 3,750 g, with a head circumference of 33 cm, and a height of 51 cm. The patient's Apgar score was 8 at 1 minute, and 9 at 5 minutes after birth. He had a healthy pigmentation and demonstrated a good sucking instinct. The discovery of a bilateral palpebral occlusion coupled with the observation that he did not appear to have eyeballs, prompted the patient's transfer to the Ophthalmology Department of the Center Hospital University. A subsequent examination revealed a slight bilateral introversio of the eyelid (entropion), with fine eyelids and little palpebral fissures (Figure 1). Spacing the eyelids with a pediatric speculum showed an emptiness of the orbital cavities which were reduced. An emergency clinical assessment (including cardiovascular, pulmonary pleura, genitourinary, and neurological tests) was requested. Paraclinical testing, comprising cerebral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); an orbital frontal brain scan; an ocular ultrasound; and thoracoabdominal, face, and chest radiography; was carried out to search for associated congenital malformations. MRI and the patient's karyotype could not be ascertained due to lack of equipment. The ocular ultrasound (Figure 2), as well as the orbital brain CT scan (Figure 3), showed severe right-side microphthalmia (presence of an optic vesicle filling the orbital cavity, with a visible optic nerve and rectus muscles), and associated left eye anophthalmia (empty orbital cavity).
This case report followed the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Center Hospital University of Bouake. Consent was obtained from the parents of the newborn.

subjective.chief_complaint: A term male newborn delivered in Bouake, Ivory Coast, presented at birth with bilateral palpebral occlusion and clinically apparent absence of eyeballs.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Delivered at 39 weeks' gestation via cesarean section (birth weight 3,750 g, length 51 cm, head circumference 33 cm, Apgar scores 8 and 9), the newborn was immediately noted to have bilateral eyelid occlusion and seemingly empty orbits, prompting urgent transfer to the ophthalmology department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born to a 30-year-old mother (G4P2, history of one spontaneous abortion at 17 weeks) with sickle cell trait (HbAS, S=79%) who attended 9 prenatal visits with normal reported prenatal ultrasounds and no medication, toxin, or radiation exposures. Maternal prenatal infectious screening was positive for rubella IgG (13 IU/mL) and Toxoplasma IgG (14 IU/mL), and negative for syphilis (TPHA and VDRL negative), HBV, HCV, and HIV.
subjective.review_of_systems: Healthy skin pigmentation and intact sucking reflex; bilateral absence of visible globes.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic examination revealed bilateral mild entropion with narrow, small palpebral fissures; separation of the eyelids with a pediatric speculum revealed reduced, empty-appearing orbital cavities. Systemic cardiovascular, pulmonary, genitourinary, and neurological examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Maternal prenatal syphilis (TPHA, VDRL), HBV, HCV, and HIV serologies were negative. Thoracoabdominal, facial, and chest radiographs were unremarkable. Ocular B-scan ultrasonography demonstrated severe right microphthalmia (a rudimentary optic vesicle filling the right orbit with a visible optic nerve and rectus muscles) and complete left clinical anophthalmia (empty left orbital cavity).
objective.advanced_workup: Orbital and brain CT scan confirmed severe right microphthalmia and left clinical anophthalmia without intracranial malformations (brain MRI and karyotyping were unavailable).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed congenital right severe microphthalmia and left clinical anophthalmia without systemic malformations (congenital syphilis, HIV, and viral hepatitis excluded via negative maternal prenatal serologies; maternal rubella/Toxoplasma IgG positivity noted).
